Read the colour code in order: two **digits**, a **multiplier**, then the **tolerance**.
**Step 1 — recall the digit values.**
black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, **green 5**, **blue 6**, violet 7, grey 8,
white 9 ✓
**Step 2 — read the first two bands.**
green = **5**
blue = **6**
giving the two significant figures **56**
**Step 3 — read the multiplier.** Brown as a multiplier means **x 10¹** ✓
56 x 10 = **560 Ω**
**Step 4 — read the tolerance.** Gold is ±5%, **silver is ±10%** ✓
**Step 5 — assemble.**
**560 Ω ± 10%** ✓
so the true value lies between 504 Ω and 616 Ω.
**The mnemonic for the digits.** "**B B ROY of Great Britain had a Very Good Wife**" -
Black, Brown, Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Violet, Grey, White, for 0 to 9 ✓
**The tolerance band, separately.** Only two colours are common there:
**gold = ±5%**, **silver = ±10%** ✓
and their position, set slightly apart from the others, identifies which end of the
resistor to read from.
**Why the third band is a multiplier, not a digit.** A four-band resistor encodes its
value as **two digits x a power of ten** ✓ Brown is 1 as a digit and 10¹ as a
multiplier - the same colour, different roles depending on position.
**A check on plausibility.** 560 Ω is a standard preferred value in the E12 series ✓ so
is 56 Ω, but 5600 Ω would need a **red** third band, not brown.
**Reading the distractors.** **56 Ω ± 5%** ✗ ignores the multiplier and misreads silver
as gold. **560 Ω ± 5%** ✗ has the value right but the tolerance wrong. **5600 Ω ± 10%**
✗ uses red as the multiplier ✓
∴ 560 Ω ± 10%.

A wire **moving** in a field generates a current, and the rule for its direction is
**Fleming's right hand rule**.
**Step 1 — recall the rule.** Hold the **thumb, forefinger and middle finger** of the
**right** hand mutually perpendicular:
**ForeFinger** → **Field** B
**ThuMb** → **Motion** of the conductor
**Middle finger** → **Induced current** ✓
**Step 2 — see why the right hand.** This is a **generator** situation: mechanical
motion is producing electricity ✓ The right hand is for generators; the left is for
motors.
**The distinction worth fixing.**
**right hand** → **generator**: given motion and field, find the **induced** current ✓
**left hand** → **motor**: given current and field, find the **force** on the wire ✓
Both have the same finger assignments; only the hand changes.
**Why the rule gives the right answer.** The induced current must, by **Lenz's law**,
oppose the motion that produces it ✓ Fleming's right hand rule is simply a convenient
geometric packaging of that principle, together with F = qv̄ x B̄ acting on the charges
in the moving wire.
**The underlying physics.** A charge q in the wire moves with it at velocity v through
field B, so it feels a force qv̄ x B̄ **along** the wire ✓ That force drives the charges
to one end, setting up the emf - and its direction is exactly what the right hand rule
reproduces.
**Why the other rules do not apply.**
**Fleming's left hand rule** ✗ gives the **force** on a current-carrying wire - the
motor rule, the converse problem.
**Right hand clasp rule** (and **Ampere's rule**) ✗ give the direction of the magnetic
**field around a current**, not an induced current ✓ Grip the wire with the right hand,
thumb along the current, and the fingers curl the way B circles.
**The magnitude, for completeness.** For a rod of length l moving at v perpendicular to
B,
**emf = Bvl** ✓ while the right hand rule supplies the sign.
∴ Fleming's right hand rule.

Equal voltages across all three elements means the circuit is at **resonance**; then
doubling R halves the current.
**Step 1 — read the initial state.** V_R = V_L = V_C = **20 V** ✓
Since V_L = V_C, the reactances are equal, so the circuit is **at resonance** and
X_L = X_C ✓
**Step 2 — find the supply voltage.** At resonance the reactive voltages cancel:
V = √(V_R² + (V_L − V_C)²)
= √(20² + 0)
= **20 V** ✓
**Step 3 — double the resistance.** The source voltage and frequency are unchanged, so
the circuit is still at resonance and
Z′ = R′ = **2R**
I′ = V/Z′ = 20/(2R) = **I/2** ✓ the current is halved.
**Step 4 — find the new voltages.**
across R′: V_R′ = I′R′ = (I/2)(2R) = **IR = 20 V** - unchanged ✓
across L: V_L′ = I′X_L = (I/2)X_L = **10 V** ✓
across C: V_C′ = I′X_C = (I/2)X_C = **10 V** ✓
**Step 5 — state the answer.** **20 V, 10 V, 10 V** ✓
**Why V_R stays at 20 V.** At resonance the whole supply voltage appears across the
resistor, whatever its value ✓ Doubling R halves the current, and the product IR is
unchanged - the resistor always takes the full 20 V.
**Why the reactive voltages halve.** X_L and X_C depend only on L, C and the frequency,
none of which has changed ✓ So with half the current flowing, half the voltage appears
across each.
**A check on the total.**
√(20² + (10 − 10)²) = **20 V** ✓ matching the supply, as it must.
**What has changed in practice.** The circuit is now **less sharply** resonant: the
quality factor Q = X_L/R has halved, so the voltage magnification across L and C is
smaller ✓ That magnification - here 20/20 = 1 before and 10/20 = 0·5 after - is exactly
what Q measures.
**Reading the distractors.** **20, 20, 20** ✗ ignores the change altogether. **20, 40,
40** ✗ doubles the reactive voltages, as if the current had risen. **10, 20, 20** ✗
halves the wrong one ✓
∴ 20 V, 10 V, 10 V.

Two digit bands, a multiplier and a tolerance - read in that order.
**Step 1 — read the digits.**
green = **5**
black = **0**
giving **50**
**Step 2 — read the multiplier.** Violet as a multiplier is **x 10⁷** ✓
50 x 10⁷ = 5 x 10⁸ Ω
= **500 MΩ**
**Step 3 — read the tolerance.** Gold = **±5%** ✓
**Step 4 — assemble.**
**500 ± 5% MΩ** ✓
so the value lies between 475 MΩ and 525 MΩ.
**The colour values again.** black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue
6, **violet 7**, grey 8, white 9 ✓ and the same sequence serves as powers of ten for the
multiplier band.
**Converting the powers.**
50 x 10⁷ Ω = 500 x 10⁶ Ω = **500 MΩ** ✓
since 1 MΩ = 10⁶ Ω. Keeping track of that step is where the arithmetic usually goes
astray.
**Why 500 MΩ is a plausible value.** Half a gigaohm is very high but perfectly real ✓
Such resistors appear in electrometers, insulation testers and the input stages of
sensitive amplifiers.
**Why the tolerance must be quoted.** A resistor is manufactured to a nominal value with
a stated spread ✓ A ±5% part marked 500 MΩ is guaranteed only to lie within 25 MΩ of it,
and the band exists so that can be read at a glance.
**Reading the distractors.** **50 MΩ** ✗ uses violet as 10⁶ rather than 10⁷. **500 MΩ**
with no tolerance ✗ ignores the gold band - a correct value but an incomplete answer, and
the question's options distinguish the two. **500 ± 10% MΩ** ✗ reads gold as silver ✓
∴ 500 ± 5% MΩ.

Reduce the parallel pair, add the internal resistance, then apply Ohm's law to the whole
circuit.
**Step 1 — combine the two resistors in parallel.**
R_p = (2 x 6)/(2 + 6)
= 12/8
= **1·5 Ω** ✓
less than either branch, as a parallel combination must be.
**Step 2 — add the internal resistance.** It is in **series** with the external
combination:
R_total = 1·5 + 0·5
= **2 Ω**
**Step 3 — find the current through the battery.**
I = E/R_total
= 2/2
= **1 A** ✓
**Why the internal resistance must be included.** The current flows through the cell as
well as the external circuit ✓ Leaving out the 0·5 Ω would give 2/1·5 = 1·33 A - which
is the second distractor, and the commonest error here.
**The terminal voltage of the cell.**
V = E − I r
= 2 − (1)(0·5)
= **1·5 V** ✓
which is also the voltage across the parallel combination - consistent, since
1·5 V ÷ 1·5 Ω = 1 A ✓
**How the current splits.**
through the 2 Ω: 1·5/2 = **0·75 A**
through the 6 Ω: 1·5/6 = **0·25 A**
total: **1 A** ✓ as required. The smaller resistor takes three times the current, in
inverse proportion to the resistances.
**Where the energy goes.** Of the 2 W delivered by the emf, 0·5 W is lost inside the cell
and **1·5 W** reaches the external resistors ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **4/3 A** ✗ omits the internal resistance. **4 A** ✗ would
need a total of 0·5 Ω. **4/17 A** ✗ comes from adding resistances incorrectly ✓
∴ 1 A.

The series value gives the **sum**, and the parallel value with it gives the
**product** - so the two resistances are roots of a quadratic.
**Step 1 — write the two conditions.**
a + b = **6**
ab/(a + b) = **4/3**
**Step 2 — find the product.**
ab = (4/3)(a + b)
= (4/3)(6)
= **8**
**Step 3 — form the quadratic.** The two resistances are the roots of
x² − (sum)x + product = 0
x² − 6x + 8 = 0
**Step 4 — factorise.**
(x − 4)(x − 2) = 0
**x = 4 Ω and 2 Ω** ✓
**Step 5 — verify.**
series: 4 + 2 = **6 Ω** ✓
parallel: (4 x 2)/6 = 8/6 = **4/3 Ω** ✓ both conditions met.
**The useful identity.** For any two resistances,
(series value) x (parallel value) = **ab**, their product ✓
Here 6 x 4/3 = 8, which is what turns the problem into a quadratic in one line.
**Why the parallel value must be smaller than both.** 4/3 Ω is below 2 Ω and 4 Ω ✓ a
sanity check that the data are consistent before any algebra.
**Testing the distractors quickly.**
**8 Ω, 1 Ω** ✗ - series 9, not 6
**4 Ω, 6 Ω** ✗ - series 10
**6 Ω, 2 Ω** ✗ - series 8 ✓
Only one pair sums to 6, and checking the sum alone eliminates the other three.
**The general method.** Whenever two unknowns are given through their **sum** and
**product**, write x² − Sx + P = 0 ✓ It is the same technique that solves "two numbers
add to 6 and multiply to 8", and it appears throughout physics problems of this kind.
**A note on when no solution exists.** The quadratic has real roots only if S² ≥ 4P ✓
Here 36 ≥ 32, so the data are physically realisable - a parallel value much closer to
S/4 would not be.
∴ 4 Ω, 2 Ω.

A reversed cell **subtracts** its emf, but its internal resistance still **adds**.
**Step 1 — work out the net emf.** Three cells are correctly connected and one is
reversed, so the reversed one opposes the others:
E_net = 3E − E
= **2E** ✓
**Step 2 — work out the total internal resistance.** Resistance does not care which way
a cell is turned round ✓ All four internal resistances remain in series:
r_net = 4r ✓
**Step 3 — state the answer.** **2E and 4r** ✓
**Why the emf loses two cells' worth, not one.** The reversed cell not only fails to
contribute its own E, it actively **cancels** one of the others ✓ The loss is 2E,
which is why four cells with one reversed behave like **two** cells, not three.
**Why the internal resistance is unaffected.** r is a property of the cell's chemistry
and construction ✓ It dissipates energy whichever way the current passes through it, so
all four add in series regardless of orientation.
**The general rule.** With n cells in series of which m are reversed,
E_net = (n − 2m)E and r_net = **nr** ✓
Here n = 4, m = 1, giving 2E and 4r.
**A worked instance.** Four 1·5 V cells, each 0·5 Ω, with one reversed, driving a 2 Ω
load:
E_net = **3·0 V**, r_net = **2·0 Ω**
I = 3/(2 + 2) = **0·75 A** ✓
against 6/(2 + 2) = 1·5 A had all four been correct - the current is **halved**.
**How to spot a reversed cell in practice.** The battery is weak but still warm, and the
reversed cell **discharges faster** than the rest and may leak ✓ It is being driven
backwards by the others.
**Reading the distractors.** **4E and 4r** ✗ assumes all four aid. **4E and 2r** ✗ and
**2E and 2r** ✗ both reduce the internal resistance, which reversing a cell cannot do ✓
That last point is the heart of the question.
∴ 2E and 4r.
